column6: Nach zwei Monaten bekam sie starkes Heimweh.
column7: After two months she got badly homesick.
column8: The opposite of Fernweh ('wanderlust'), Heimweh, literally 'home-pain', reflects the German tension between wanting to travel and wanting to belong.

column7: May I smoke here?
column8: Unlike English 'can', German has separate modal verbs for ability (können), permission (dürfen), and social obligation (sollen).

column6: Wegen des Regens bleiben wir zu Hause.
column7: Because of the rain, we're staying home.
column8: 'Wegen' technically takes the genitive, but in speech it's increasingly used with the dative: linguists call this 'Genitiverosion'.

column6: Ich lerne seit drei Jahren Deutsch.
column7: I've been learning German for three years.
column8: 'Seit' always takes the dative and pairs with the present tense for actions still ongoing — the same logic as English 'for'.

column6: Obwohl es regnet, gehen wir spazieren.
column7: Although it's raining, we're going for a walk.
column8: 'Obwohl' sends the verb to the end of the clause: the Verbendstellung rule reflects German's preference for laying out the whole context before the action.

column6: Die Stimmung auf dem Fest war ausgezeichnet.
column7: The mood at the party was excellent.
column8: Stimmung comes from 'Stimme' (voice, tuning): it originally described a tuned instrument, later the collective emotional tone of a group.

column7: He quit smoking.
column8: In the Perfekt, separable verbs insert 'ge-' between the prefix and the stem: 'aufgehört'.

column6: Ich bringe meiner Familie ein Mitbringsel aus Berlin mit.
column7: I'm bringing my family a small souvenir from Berlin.
column8: Bringing a Mitbringsel back from a trip, or when visiting someone's home, is a strong social norm in Germany.

column6: Der Arzt hat mir ein Medikament verschrieben.
column7: The doctor prescribed me a medication.
column8: Prescriptions are tightly regulated in Germany: many over-the-counter drugs elsewhere require a 'Rezept' here.

column6: Nach dem Feierabend treffe ich Freunde.
column7: After work I'm meeting friends.
column8: Feierabend, literally 'celebration evening', reflects the German idea that the end of the workday is a moment worth honoring.

column5: to be glad / to look forward to
column6: Ich freue mich auf das Wochenende.
column7: I'm looking forward to the weekend.
column8: 'Sich freuen auf' looks to the future, 'sich freuen über' to the present or past — two prepositions for two timeframes.

column6: Es war spät, trotzdem sind wir noch spazieren gegangen.
column7: It was late, but we went for a walk anyway.
column8: At the start of a sentence, 'trotzdem' counts as the first element and pushes the subject after the verb: the verb-second rule.

column6: Ich muss einen neuen Ausweis beantragen.
column7: I have to apply for a new ID card.
column8: In Germany almost everything official is 'beantragt' with a form: the verb instantly evokes bureaucracy.

column6: Sie hat ein Jahr im Ausland gelebt.
column7: She lived abroad for a year.
column8: 'Ausland' is the opposite of 'Inland'. You say 'im Ausland' (where) and 'ins Ausland' (to where); it has no plural.

column6: Er hat sich über den Lärm beschwert.
column7: He complained about the noise.
column8: In Germany, a formal written complaint ('Beschwerde') is seen as a legitimate right, not as impoliteness.

column6: Früh aufzustehen ist bei mir zur Gewohnheit geworden.
column7: Getting up early has become a habit for me.
column8: The suffix '-heit', like '-keit' and '-ung', forms abstract feminine nouns: 'gewohnt' → 'Gewohnheit'.

column6: Ich schreibe es auf, damit ich es nicht vergesse.
column7: I'm writing it down so I don't forget it.
column8: 'Damit' as a conjunction sends the verb to the end; as an adverb ('with that') it doesn't — same word, two behaviors.

column5: to get done / to take care of
column6: Ich muss noch ein paar Dinge erledigen.
column7: I still have a few things to take care of.
column8: 'Alles erledigt' ('all done') is an almost satisfying phrase in German: the to-do list is practically a cultural genre.

column6: Ich habe einen Vorschlag für das Wochenende.
column7: I have a suggestion for the weekend.
column8: In German meetings, every 'Vorschlag' is calmly weighed first: deciding without discussion is seen as rushed.

column6: Wir haben einen gemütlichen Abend zu Hause verbracht.
column7: We spent a cosy evening at home.
column8: 'Gemütlich' describes not just a warm place but also an unhurried pace: 'mach's dir gemütlich' means 'make yourself comfortable'.

column6: Der Umzug in die neue Wohnung war anstrengend.
column7: The move to the new apartment was exhausting.
column8: In Germany, friends often help with a move and are rewarded with pizza and beer — jokingly called being 'paid in beer'.

column6: Können Sie mir ein gutes Restaurant empfehlen?
column7: Can you recommend a good restaurant?
column8: 'Empfehlen' takes the dative of the person and the accusative of the thing: 'ich empfehle dir das Buch' (I recommend you the book).

column6: Während ich koche, deckst du den Tisch.
column7: While I cook, you set the table.
column8: 'Während' is both a conjunction (verb at the end) and a preposition with the genitive ('während des Essens') — a true grammatical wildcard.

column6: Sie hat viel Erfahrung in diesem Bereich.
column7: She has a lot of experience in this field.
column8: On German CVs, 'Berufserfahrung' is listed in reverse chronological order, with dates precise to the month.

column6: Ich habe mich für den blauen Mantel entschieden.
column7: I've decided on the blue coat.
column8: 'Sich entscheiden für' indicates the choice made; 'sich entscheiden zu' the action decided on — the preposition changes the meaning.

column6: Ich habe dir eine Nachricht geschickt.
column7: I sent you a message.
column8: In the plural, 'die Nachrichten' means the TV news: the 8pm 'Tagesschau' is Europe's oldest and most-watched.

column6: Du musst unbedingt dieses Museum besuchen.
column7: You absolutely must visit this museum.
column8: 'Unbedingt' literally means 'without condition': advice given with 'unbedingt' is almost a friendly order.

column6: Wir sparen für eine große Reise.
column7: We're saving up for a big trip.
column8: The German household savings rate is among Europe's highest: the 'Sparbuch' (savings book) is a childhood ritual for many.

column6: Der Zug hat zwanzig Minuten Verspätung.
column7: The train is running twenty minutes late.
column8: With over 60 minutes' delay, Deutsche Bahn refunds part of the ticket: 'Fahrgastrechte' (passenger rights) claims are almost a national sport.

column6: Ich kann mir gut vorstellen, in Wien zu leben.
column7: I can easily imagine living in Vienna.
column8: With the dative ('sich etwas vorstellen') it means to imagine; with the accusative ('sich vorstellen') it means to introduce oneself. The case changes everything.

column6: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin.
column7: I'm staying home because I'm sick.
column8: 'Weil' sends the verb to the end of the subordinate clause, the same rule as 'obwohl' and 'dass'.

column6: Ich glaube, dass es morgen regnet.
column7: I believe it will rain tomorrow.
column8: 'Dass' introduces object clauses and always sends the conjugated verb to the end of the sentence.

column6: Wenn es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause.
column7: If it rains, we'll stay home.
column8: 'Wenn' is used both for hypothetical conditions and for repeated actions over time, unlike 'als' for a single past event.

column6: Als ich klein war, wohnte ich in Rom.
column7: When I was little, I lived in Rome.
column8: 'Als' is used only for a single event in the past, never for habitual actions, where 'wenn' is used instead.

column6: Räum dein Zimmer auf, bevor du gehst.
column7: Tidy your room before you go.
column8: 'Bevor' sends the verb to the end of the subordinate clause, like all German subordinating conjunctions.

column6: Nachdem wir gegessen hatten, gingen wir spazieren.
column7: After we had eaten, we went for a walk.
column8: 'Nachdem' often requires the Plusquamperfekt in the subordinate clause when its action precedes the main one.

column6: Ich rufe dich an, sobald ich ankomme.
column7: I'll call you as soon as I arrive.
column8: 'Sobald' introduces an immediately following action, often used for promises or concrete plans.

column6: Falls es regnet, nehmen wir einen Schirm mit.
column7: In case it rains, we'll bring an umbrella.
column8: 'Falls' is more hypothetical than 'wenn': it suggests a less certain possibility, almost a precaution.

column5: so that / with the result that
column6: Er war müde, sodass er früh schlafen ging.
column7: He was tired, so he went to bed early.
column8: 'Sodass' introduces a consequence, unlike 'damit', which introduces an intentional purpose.

column6: Ich weiß nicht, ob er kommt.
column7: I don't know whether he's coming.
column8: 'Ob' introduces indirect questions and is different from 'wenn', which is never used in this context.

column6: Er lernte Deutsch, indem er viel las.
column7: He learned German by reading a lot.
column8: 'Indem' describes the means by which a result is achieved — a structure typical of more formal registers.

column6: Obgleich es spät war, arbeitete sie weiter.
column7: Although it was late, she kept working.
column8: 'Obgleich' is a more formal, literary variant of 'obwohl', used mostly in writing.

column6: Je mehr ich lerne, desto besser verstehe ich.
column7: The more I study, the better I understand.
column8: 'Je ... desto' takes the comparative in both clauses and is one of the more elegant structures of intermediate German.

column7: That's probably right.
column8: The Konjunktiv II of 'dürfen' expresses a polite supposition, more cautious than the direct indicative.

column7: That could be a problem.
column8: The Konjunktiv II of 'können' expresses a hypothetical possibility, more uncertain than the indicative 'kann'.

column7: He should be here soon.
column8: The Konjunktiv II of 'müssen' expresses a logical expectation, not a direct obligation like the indicative 'muss'.

column7: You should sleep more.
column8: The Konjunktiv II of 'sollen' is the standard form for giving advice in German, far more common than the indicative 'sollst'.

column7: I would like a coffee, please.
column8: 'Möchte' is the Konjunktiv II of 'mögen', used every day for polite requests, almost as a verb in its own right.

column7: Oh, come with us!
column8: Modal particles like 'doch' have no fixed translation: they add emotional nuance that's hard to render in another language.

column7: Expectations were high.
column8: 'Erwartung' comes from 'erwarten' (to expect), a very common inseparable verb in professional contexts.

column7: German skills are a requirement.
column8: 'Voraussetzung' comes from 'voraussetzen' (to presuppose), a compound of 'voraus' (in advance) and 'setzen' (to put).

column7: This decision has consequences.
column8: 'Konsequenz' means both 'consequence' and 'consistency' (in behavior) — two distinct meanings from the same root.

column6: Die Ursache des Problems ist unklar.
column7: The cause of the problem is unclear.
column8: 'Ursache' and 'Grund' are near-synonyms, but 'Ursache' sounds more scientific and objective, 'Grund' more personal.

column7: The medication shows a fast effect.
column8: 'Wirkung zeigen' is the standard fixed collocation used especially in medical and scientific contexts.

column7: Time is an important factor.
column8: 'Faktor' is nearly identical across many languages, a learned Latin loanword shared internationally.

column7: That's an interesting aspect.
column8: 'Aspekt' is often used in formal analysis and discussion, a slightly higher register than 'Seite' (side).

column7: I understand your standpoint.
column8: 'Standpunkt' combines 'stehen' (to stand) and 'Punkt' (point): the point from which one views an issue.

column7: That's a strong argument.
column8: 'Argument' in German only means 'logical reasoning', never 'a quarrel' — for that, German uses 'Streit'.

column7: We had a long discussion.
column8: 'Diskussion' describes an exchange of opinions, while 'Streit' implies a more heated emotional conflict.

column7: The political debate was heated.
column8: 'Debatte' is a loanword from French, used especially in public and political contexts more formal than 'Diskussion'.

column7: I completely agree with you.
column8: 'Zustimmen' takes the dative of the person you agree with: 'dir zustimmen'.

column6: Ich möchte dir nicht widersprechen, aber...
column7: I don't want to contradict you, but...
column8: 'Widersprechen' takes the dative of the person contradicted, like many verbs with the prefix 'wider-'.

column7: I reject this proposal.
column8: 'Ablehnen' is separable: 'lehne ab' in the present tense, with the prefix detached at the end of the sentence.

column7: I accept your decision.
column8: 'Akzeptieren' takes a direct accusative object with no preposition, a Latin loanword now fully naturalized.

column6: Es ist schwer, ihn zu überzeugen.
column7: It's hard to convince him.
column8: 'Überzeugen' isn't separable: it belongs to the group of verbs with the inseparable prefix 'über-'.

column7: I doubt that's true.
column8: 'Bezweifeln' takes a direct accusative object or a 'dass' clause, unlike the plain 'zweifeln an' plus dative.

column6: Ich nehme an, dass er kommt.
column7: I assume he's coming.
column8: 'Annehmen' means both 'to accept an object' and 'to assume, presume', depending on the sentence context.

column6: Ich vermute, dass es ein Missverständnis war.
column7: I suspect it was a misunderstanding.
column8: 'Vermuten' is nearly synonymous with 'annehmen' here, but suggests a slightly greater degree of uncertainty.

column6: Er behauptet, die Wahrheit zu sagen.
column7: He claims he's telling the truth.
column8: 'Behaupten' often implies some skepticism on the speaker's part about the truth of the reported claim.

column6: Ich möchte betonen, wie wichtig das ist.
column7: I'd like to emphasize how important this is.
column8: 'Betonen' comes from 'Ton' (tone, sound): literally 'to put the tone, the stress' on something.

column7: She never mentioned that.
column8: 'Erwähnen' takes a direct accusative object with no preposition, a verb very common when recounting conversations.

column6: Ich muss zugeben, dass ich mich geirrt habe.
column7: I have to admit I was wrong.
column8: 'Zugeben' is separable: 'gebe zu' in the present tense, used for admitting a mistake or an uncomfortable truth.

column7: I think you're mistaken.
column8: 'Sich irren' is reflexive and more formal than the plain 'einen Fehler machen' (to make a mistake).

column7: The teacher is correcting the homework.
column8: 'Korrigieren' takes a direct accusative object, a Latin loanword now common in school and editorial contexts.

column7: I'd like to improve my pronunciation.
column8: 'Verbessern' takes a direct accusative object and is used for both people and objects or skills.

column6: Die Firma entwickelt sich ständig weiter.
column7: The company keeps developing further.
column8: 'Sich weiterentwickeln' combines 'weiter' (further) with the reflexive 'sich entwickeln' (to develop).

column6: Ich mache eine Fortbildung im Sommer.
column7: I'm doing further training in the summer.
column8: 'Fortbildung' is distinct from 'Ausbildung': the first is continuing training for those already working, the second initial training.

column6: Diese Kompetenz ist im Beruf wichtig.
column7: This skill is important in the profession.
column8: 'Kompetenz' describes a specific, recognized skill, often used in the plural 'Kompetenzen' on CVs.

column6: Er übernimmt die Verantwortung für den Fehler.
column7: He's taking responsibility for the mistake.
column8: 'Verantwortung übernehmen' ('to take on responsibility') is the standard fixed collocation in German.

column6: Die Bäckerei liegt gegenüber der Kirche.
column7: The bakery is opposite the church.
column8: 'Gegenüber' takes the dative and can come before or after the noun: 'der Kirche gegenüber' is just as correct.

column6: Trotz des Regens gingen wir spazieren.
column7: Despite the rain, we went for a walk.
column8: 'Trotz' technically takes the genitive, but in speech it's increasingly common with the dative too.

column7: He lives outside the city.
column8: 'Außerhalb' takes the genitive and is the direct opposite of 'innerhalb' (inside, within).

column6: Bitte antworten Sie innerhalb einer Woche.
column7: Please reply within a week.
column8: 'Innerhalb' takes the genitive and is very common in administrative language and contracts.

column6: Anstatt zu telefonieren, schreibt sie eine E-Mail.
column7: Instead of calling, she writes an email.
column8: 'Anstatt' takes the genitive or the infinitive with 'zu' — both constructions are accepted in current usage.

column7: According to the report, prices are rising.
column8: 'Laut' takes the genitive or the dative depending on context and is typical of journalistic language.

column6: Dank deiner Hilfe habe ich es geschafft.
column7: Thanks to your help, I made it.
column8: 'Dank' takes the genitive or the dative, like 'laut', and always carries a positive connotation, unlike 'wegen'.

column6: Hinsichtlich der Kosten gibt es Fragen.
column7: With regard to the costs, there are questions.
column8: 'Hinsichtlich' takes the genitive and is typical of a more formal administrative or academic register.

column6: Mithilfe eines Wörterbuchs verstand ich den Text.
column7: With the help of a dictionary, I understood the text.
column8: 'Mithilfe' takes the genitive and is common in technical and academic language to describe a tool used.

column6: Ich bitte um Verzeihung für die Verspätung.
column7: I ask for forgiveness for the delay.
column8: 'Um Verzeihung bitten' is more formal than the plain 'sich entschuldigen', used in written or ceremonial contexts.

column7: I'd like to file a complaint.
column8: 'Einreichen' is separable: 'reiche ein', used for the formal submission of documents or complaints.

column7: You're entitled to a refund.
column8: 'Anspruch haben auf' takes the accusative and is typical of legal and contractual language.

column7: The refund takes two weeks.
column8: 'Erstattung' comes from 'erstatten' (to reimburse), a formal verb used especially in insurance and commercial contexts.

column6: Das Gerät hat zwei Jahre Garantie.
column7: The device has a two-year warranty.
column8: Across the whole EU, the minimum legal warranty on new products is two years, regardless of the manufacturer.

column7: The company is processing your complaint.
column8: 'Reklamation' is more formal and technical than 'Beschwerde', typically used in commercial and administrative contexts.

column6: Diese Behörde ist für Visa zuständig.
column7: This authority is responsible for visas.
column8: 'Zuständig sein für' takes the accusative and is the standard structure for stating an office's area of responsibility.

column6: Die Anmeldung muss innerhalb von zwei Wochen erfolgen.
column7: Registration must happen within two weeks.
column8: In Germany, 'Anmeldung' at the registry office is legally required within two weeks of moving.

column7: He's applying for a new residence permit.
column8: 'Beantragen' isn't separable: it belongs to the group of verbs with the inseparable prefix 'be-'.

column7: My nationality is Italian.
column8: 'Staatsangehörigkeit' is a complex compound: 'Staat' (state) + 'angehören' (to belong to) + the suffix '-keit'.

column7: Naturalisation often takes years.
column8: 'Einbürgerung' comes from 'Bürger' (citizen), with the prefix 'ein-' indicating the process of 'entering' citizenship.

column7: The employer pays social insurance.
column8: Germany's Sozialversicherung system covers pensions, unemployment, health care, and accident insurance in one framework.

column7: Unemployment has fallen sharply.
column8: 'Arbeitslosigkeit' comes from 'arbeitslos' (jobless) with the abstract suffix '-igkeit'.

column7: The German economy is growing slowly.
column8: Germany is the world's fourth-largest economy by nominal GDP, the largest in the European Union.

column6: Die Inflation macht das Leben teurer.
column7: Inflation is making life more expensive.
column8: 'Inflation' is nearly identical across languages, an internationally shared economic term.

column7: I pay taxes every year.
column8: In German, 'die Steuer' (feminine) is the tax, while 'das Steuer' (neuter) means 'steering wheel, helm' — same word, different gender.

column6: Ich habe einen Brief vom Finanzamt bekommen.
column7: I got a letter from the tax office.
column8: 'Finanzamt' combines 'Finanz' and 'Amt' (office): the authority that handles tax filings in Germany.

column7: His income has increased.
column8: 'Einkommen' comes from the verb 'einkommen' (to come in, arrive): literally 'that which comes in' financially.

column6: Unsere Ausgaben sind diesen Monat hoch.
column7: Our expenses are high this month.
column8: 'Ausgabe' comes from 'ausgeben' (to spend), the direct opposite of 'Einkommen' (income).

column6: Meine Ersparnisse reichen für den Urlaub.
column7: My savings are enough for the vacation.
column8: 'Ersparnis' comes from 'ersparen' (to save), almost always used in the plural 'Ersparnisse'.

column6: Wir haben einen Kredit für das Haus aufgenommen.
column7: We took out a loan for the house.
column8: 'Einen Kredit aufnehmen' ('to take out a loan') is the standard fixed collocation in financial contexts.

column7: They have a lot of debt.
column8: 'Schulden' is always plural in German and shares a root with 'Schuld' (guilt): debt as a financial 'fault'.

column6: Wir haben ein festes Budget für die Reise.
column7: We have a fixed budget for the trip.
column8: 'Budget' is a loanword from French/English, with a pronunciation that keeps the silent French ending.

column6: Der Umsatz ist im letzten Jahr gestiegen.
column7: Revenue rose last year.
column8: 'Umsatz' comes from 'umsetzen' (to put into circulation): a key term in German company accounts.

column6: Die Firma macht dieses Jahr Gewinn.
column7: The company is making a profit this year.
column8: 'Gewinn' means both 'business profit' and 'winnings' from gambling — two senses sharing the idea of gain.

column7: The loss was unexpected.
column8: 'Verlust' comes from 'verlieren' (to lose) and is used both financially and emotionally, as in a personal loss.

column7: This is a good investment.
column8: 'Investition' is nearly identical across languages, another Latin-derived economic term shared internationally.

column6: Der Absatzmarkt reagiert schnell auf Neuigkeiten.
column7: The sales market reacts quickly to news.
column8: 'Absatzmarkt' combines 'Absatz' (sales) and 'Markt': the market as the sum of supply and demand, not a physical place.

column6: Die Konkurrenz ist stark in dieser Branche.
column7: Competition is strong in this sector.
column8: 'Konkurrenz' is always a singular collective noun, referring to the whole body of competitors in a sector.

column7: He works in the IT industry.
column8: 'Branche' is a loanword from French, keeping the nasal ending in German pronunciation.

column7: Demand for apartments is rising.
column8: 'Nachfrage' and 'Angebot' (supply) are the classic economic pairing of demand and supply.

column6: Der Verbraucher hat viele Rechte in der EU.
column7: The consumer has many rights in the EU.
column8: 'Verbraucher' comes from 'verbrauchen' (to consume), the standard legal term used in EU regulations.

column7: This product is very popular.
column8: 'Produkt' is nearly identical across languages, one of many Latin loanwords common in commercial language.

column7: Production takes several weeks.
column8: 'Herstellung' comes from 'herstellen' (to produce, manufacture), a separable verb common in industrial contexts.

column7: The delivery arrives tomorrow.
column8: 'Lieferung' comes from 'liefern' (to deliver, supply), a verb very frequent in e-commerce.

column6: Meine Bestellung ist noch nicht angekommen.
column7: My order hasn't arrived yet.
column8: 'Bestellung' comes from 'bestellen' (to order), used both for restaurant orders and online purchases.

column6: Ich habe meinen Führerschein mit achtzehn gemacht.
column7: I got my driving licence at eighteen.
column8: Getting a licence in Germany is notoriously expensive, often over 2,000 euros between mandatory lessons and exams.

column6: Sie nimmt Stunden in der Fahrschule.
column7: She's taking lessons at the driving school.
column8: In Germany, both practical and theory driving lessons are mandatory and fairly rigorous.

column6: Zum Glück gab es keinen Unfall.
column7: Luckily there was no accident.
column8: 'Zum Glück' ('luckily') is one of the most common opening expressions for expressing relief.

column7: The tyre is flat.
column8: 'Platt' describes a flat or punctured tyre, a very specific colloquial adjective.

column6: Die nächste Tankstelle ist fünf Kilometer entfernt.
column7: The next petrol station is five kilometers away.
column8: On many German highways, fuel prices vary hugely from one station to the next — it's worth comparing.

column7: We still need to refuel.
column8: 'Tanken' takes a direct accusative object when specifying the fuel type: 'Diesel tanken' (to fill up with diesel).

column7: I don't know this traffic sign.
column8: 'Verkehrszeichen' combines 'Verkehr' (traffic) and 'Zeichen' (sign): a transparent compound typical of technical language.

column7: You can't overtake here.
column8: In the sense of 'to overtake' it is inseparable and stressed on the stem: 'er überholt', 'hat überholt' (no 'ge-').

column7: She had to brake suddenly.
column8: 'Bremsen' is regular and shares a root with 'Bremse' (brake), the corresponding noun.

column7: The speed here is limited.
column8: On many stretches of the German Autobahn there's no speed limit, but the 50 km/h city limit on normal roads is strictly enforced.

column6: Er musste ein hohes Bußgeld zahlen.
column7: He had to pay a hefty fine.
column8: 'Bußgeld' combines 'Buße' (penance, fine) and 'Geld' (money): literally 'money as penance'.

column7: We're buying a used car.
column8: 'Gebrauchtwagen' comes from 'gebraucht' (used, past participle of 'gebrauchen') plus 'Wagen' (car).

column7: This software is free.
column8: 'Software' stays feminine in German by analogy with 'die Ware' (goods), even though English has no grammatical gender.

column7: I saved the file.
column8: 'Datei' is a German word invented in the 1970s specifically for the English computing term 'file'.

column6: Vergiss nicht, das Dokument zu speichern.
column7: Don't forget to save the document.
column8: 'Speichern' comes from 'Speicher' (storage, memory): literally 'to store' data in memory.

column6: Ich habe die Datei versehentlich gelöscht.
column7: I accidentally deleted the file.
column8: 'Löschen' means both 'to delete data' and 'to put out a fire' — the common idea is 'to make disappear'.

column6: Ich lade die App gerade herunter.
column7: I'm downloading the app right now.
column8: 'Herunterladen' is separable: 'lade herunter' in the present tense, with the long prefix detached at the end.

column6: Ich lade die Fotos auf die Cloud hoch.
column7: I'm uploading the photos to the cloud.
column8: 'Hochladen' is the exact opposite of 'herunterladen', formed with the prefix 'hoch-' (up) instead of 'herunter-' (down).

column7: I forgot my password.
column8: 'Passwort' is a calque of English 'password': 'Pass' (pass, permit) + 'Wort' (word). The plural is 'Passwörter'.

column7: Enter your username.
column8: 'Eingeben' is separable and means 'to enter, type in', often used in digital interfaces.

column6: Datenschutz ist in Deutschland sehr wichtig.

column7: We haven't booked accommodation yet.
column8: 'Unterkunft' is the generic term for any kind of accommodation, from a hotel to a hostel.

column7: We're staying overnight in a youth hostel.
column8: The concept of the Jugendherberge was invented in Germany in 1909 by Richard Schirrmann, an elementary school teacher.

column6: Die Rezeption ist rund um die Uhr besetzt.
column7: Reception is staffed around the clock.
column8: 'Rund um die Uhr' ('all the way around the clock') is the idiom for '24 hours a day'.

column6: Wir checken um vierzehn Uhr ein.
column7: We're checking in at two o'clock.
column8: 'Einchecken' is a hybrid loanword from English, integrated into German separable-verb grammar.

column6: Wir müssen um elf Uhr auschecken.
column7: We have to check out at eleven.
column8: Like 'einchecken', 'auschecken' is also separable and follows the same grammatical structure.

column7: We're ordering something from room service.
column8: 'Beim Zimmerservice bestellen' takes the dative after 'bei', the standard preposition for 'from, at'.

column6: Wir machen eine Rundreise durch Süddeutschland.
column7: We're doing a tour through southern Germany.
column8: 'Durch' takes the accusative: 'durch Süddeutschland', describing movement through a region.

column7: Today we are visiting the cathedral.
column8: 'Besichtigen' is for places and buildings you go to see (cathedral, museum, flat); 'besuchen' is mostly for people or a general visit.

column7: The city tour lasts two hours.
column8: 'Stadtführung' combines 'Stadt' and 'Führung' (guidance): an organized tour with a tour guide.

column6: Wir haben die Reise über einen Reiseveranstalter gebucht.
column7: We booked the trip through a tour operator.
column8: 'Über' takes the accusative when indicating a channel: 'über einen Reiseveranstalter buchen' (to book through a tour operator).

column7: A package holiday is often cheaper.
column8: 'Pauschal' means 'flat-rate, all-inclusive': a single price covering flight, hotel, and sometimes meals.

column6: Ich schließe immer eine Reiseversicherung ab.
column7: I always take out travel insurance.
column8: 'Abschließen' is separable and takes the accusative: 'eine Versicherung abschließen' is the fixed collocation for taking out insurance.

column6: Die Zeitverschiebung nach New York beträgt sechs Stunden.
column7: The time difference to New York is six hours.
column8: 'Zeitverschiebung' is the clock difference between two places; the resulting tiredness is called 'Jetlag'.

column6: Nach dem Umzug hatte sie einen echten Kulturschock.
column7: After the move, she had real culture shock.
column8: 'Kulturschock' describes the initial disorientation of living in a country with very different cultural norms.

column7: Many emigrants move to Canada.
column8: 'Auswanderer' comes from 'auswandern' (to emigrate), the direct opposite of 'Einwanderer' (immigrant).

column7: Germany has taken in many immigrants.
column8: 'Aufnehmen' is separable and means 'to take in', a verb common in political discourse on immigration.

column6: Sie spricht fließend Deutsch und Englisch.
column7: She speaks German and English fluently.
column8: 'Fließend' as an adverb describes a very high level of linguistic fluency, close to native.

column7: Our children are growing up bilingual.
column8: 'Aufwachsen' is separable and means 'to grow up' — a typical verb when talking about childhood.

column6: Am Anfang gab es eine Sprachbarriere.
column7: At the beginning there was a language barrier.
column8: 'Sprachbarriere' combines 'Sprache' and 'Barriere' (barrier), a term very common in integration contexts.

column7: Can you interpret for us?
column8: 'Dolmetschen' describes spoken interpreting, different from 'übersetzen', which refers to written translation.

column6: Bei der Konferenz gibt es Simultanübersetzung.
column7: At the conference there's simultaneous translation.
column8: Large institutions like the European Parliament employ professional simultaneous interpreters for dozens of languages.

column7: That was a lucky coincidence.
column8: 'Zufall' comes from 'zufallen' (to fall to): literally something that 'falls onto you' unforeseen.

column7: Some people believe in fate.
column8: 'Glauben an' always takes the accusative: 'an das Schicksal' — a structure used to express belief or conviction.

column7: This is a rare opportunity.
column8: 'Gelegenheit' is nearly synonymous with 'Chance', but sounds slightly more formal and less colloquial.

column6: Ich habe den Zug leider verpasst.
column7: Unfortunately I missed the train.
column8: 'Verpassen' is used both for transport and for opportunities: 'eine Gelegenheit verpassen' (to miss an opportunity).

column7: We should make use of this opportunity.
column8: 'Nutzen' takes a direct accusative object and is nearly synonymous with the more common 'benutzen'.

column6: Er riskiert viel mit dieser Entscheidung.
column7: He's risking a lot with this decision.
column8: 'Riskieren' is a loanword from French/Italian 'rischiare', conjugated regularly in German.

column6: Manchmal muss man ein Risiko eingehen.
column7: Sometimes you have to take a risk.
column8: 'Eingehen' is separable and takes the accusative: 'ein Risiko eingehen' is the standard fixed collocation.

column7: We need to protect ourselves financially.
column8: 'Sich absichern' is reflexive and often takes the genitive or a preposition depending on the specific context.

column6: Jeder muss die Konsequenzen seiner Taten tragen.
column7: Everyone must bear the consequences of their actions.
column8: 'Tragen' means both 'to physically carry' and, figuratively, 'to bear, endure'.

column6: Es hilft, manchmal die Perspektive zu wechseln.
column7: Sometimes it helps to change perspective.
column8: 'Wechseln' takes a direct accusative object and is used both for perspectives and for concrete things like clothes or currency.

column7: Self-reflection helps with important decisions.
column8: 'Selbstreflexion' combines 'selbst' (self) and 'Reflexion' (reflection), a term increasingly used in personal-growth contexts.

column7: The quality of life here is high.
column8: Several German cities, like Munich and Düsseldorf, regularly appear in international quality-of-life rankings.

column7: Contentment is more important than wealth.
column8: 'Zufriedenheit' comes from 'zufrieden' (satisfied) with the abstract suffix '-heit'.

column6: Manche suchen ihr Leben lang nach dem Sinn des Lebens.
column7: Some people search their whole life for the meaning of life.
column8: 'Suchen nach' takes the dative: 'nach dem Sinn' — a common fixed structure for expressing a search.

column6: Mit dem Alter kommt oft Weisheit.
column7: Wisdom often comes with age.
column8: 'Weisheit' comes from 'weise' (wise) with the abstract suffix '-heit', very productive in German.

column6: In stressigen Situationen versuche ich, Gelassenheit zu bewahren.
column7: In stressful situations, I try to stay calm.
column8: 'Bewahren' takes a direct accusative object and means 'to preserve, maintain', often used for emotional states.

column7: Yoga fosters inner balance.
column8: 'Ausgeglichenheit' comes from 'ausgeglichen' (balanced), the participle of 'ausgleichen' (to balance, offset).

column6: Sie hat große innere Stärke gezeigt.
column7: She showed great inner strength.
column8: 'Zeigen' takes a direct accusative object: 'Stärke zeigen' is a common collocation for describing resilience.

column7: Resilience helps in overcoming crises.
column8: 'Resilienz' is a relatively recent term in German, borrowed from international psychological language.

column6: Achtung vor der Natur ist wichtig.
column7: Respect for nature is important.
column8: 'Achtung vor' takes the dative: 'vor der Natur' — a very common structure in environmental and civic discourse.

column6: Er sprach mit großer Demut über seinen Erfolg.
column7: He spoke about his success with great humility.
column8: 'Demut' is a higher-register term, often used in religious or philosophical contexts.

column7: Curiosity drives many scientists.
column8: 'Antreiben' is separable and means 'to drive, motivate', often used to describe motivating forces.

column7: Creativity can't be forced.
column8: 'Sich erzwingen lassen' with a negation means 'cannot be forced' — a reflexive passive-like structure.

column6: Die Reise war eine große Inspiration für sie.
column7: The trip was a great source of inspiration for her.
column8: 'Inspiration' is nearly identical across languages, another shared Latin loanword.

column7: A marathon requires a lot of stamina.
column8: 'Ausdauer' combines 'aus' and 'dauern' (to last): literally 'the ability to last all the way through'.

column7: Traveling builds self-confidence.
column8: 'Selbstvertrauen' combines 'selbst' and 'Vertrauen' (trust): different from 'Selbstbewusstsein', which is more about awareness.

column5: joy of life / zest for life
column6: Sie strahlt eine ansteckende Lebensfreude aus.
column7: She radiates an infectious zest for life.
column8: 'Lebensfreude' = 'Leben' + 'Freude': joy of living as a lasting positive energy. Also: 'voller Lebensfreude'.

column6: Der Umzug war für sie ein echter Neuanfang.
column7: The move was a real fresh start for her.
column8: 'Neuanfang' combines 'neu' (new) and 'Anfang' (beginning): a simple but very common compound for life changes.

column7: Everyone has their own life path.
column8: 'Lebensweg' combines 'Leben' (life) and 'Weg' (path, way): the path metaphor applied to existence.

column6: Der Abschluss war ihre größte Errungenschaft.
column7: Graduating was her greatest achievement.
column8: 'Errungenschaft' comes from 'erringen' (to attain through effort): a milestone reached through hard work and merit.

column7: The doctor is making a diagnosis.
column8: 'Eine Diagnose stellen' ('to make a diagnosis') is the standard fixed collocation used in medical contexts.

column6: Die Feuchtigkeit im Keller ist ein Problem.
column7: The damp in the cellar is a problem.
column8: 'Feuchtigkeit' comes from 'feucht' (damp) with the abstract suffix '-igkeit', a variant of '-keit'.

column7: He works on the assembly line.
column8: 'Fließband' combines 'fließen' (to flow) and 'Band' (belt): literally a 'flowing belt'.

column7: The climate is changing fast.
column8: 'Klima' is neuter (das Klima) and means the climate of a region; 'Wetter' is today's weather. 'Klimawandel' is climate change.

column6: Ohne Kompass finden wir den Weg nicht.
column7: Without a compass we can't find the way.
column8: 'Kompass' is masculine and ends in a double 's'. It is also used figuratively: 'ein moralischer Kompass'.

column6: Auf unserem Dach erzeugen wir Solarenergie.
column7: We produce solar energy on our roof.
column8: 'Solarenergie' is energy from the sun; the system on the roof is a 'Solaranlage' or 'Photovoltaikanlage'.

column7: I see my reflection.
column8: 'Spiegelbild' combines 'Spiegel' (mirror) and 'Bild' (image): the image reflected in a mirror.

column6: Ich würde gern in Berlin leben.
column7: I would love to live in Berlin.
column8: 'Würde + infinitive' is the most common way to express Konjunktiv II in speech, instead of rarer forms like 'lebte'.

column6: An deiner Stelle hätte ich anders reagiert.
column7: In your place, I would have reacted differently.
column8: 'Hätte' and 'wäre' are among the few Konjunktiv II forms still alive in speech: saying 'ich würde haben' sounds awkward.
